synthesis.headline: The south-central heat ridge holds through the weekend as northern-stream storms ring its flank — but the medium range finally flattens the pattern and retreats the ridge toward the Southwest
synthesis.narrative:
The amplified summer pattern Tlaloc has tracked for more than a week runs on, now clearly organized around two things at once: a durable heat ridge over the southern tier and an active northern-stream corridor draped along a slow, wavy front. At 500 mb the dominant feature is still a broad, high-amplitude ridge crowning the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes (core near 588 dam), with the warmest mid-level air over the Ohio Valley. The heat itself, however, has consolidated south of the ridge apex: WPC has a dangerous heat dome building from the Desert Southwest through the Central Plains into the Southeast, with heat indices of 105-115 and record-challenging warmth, convective suppression there coming from midlevel subsidence and warming, a strong cap and dry air aloft rather than from the modest Gulf and Atlantic surface highs. On the ridge's western side the cooldown advertised yesterday has arrived — WPC has below-normal temperatures spreading across the West today and Thursday, with Montana near the Canadian border potentially reaching its coldest levels since June. That cool, dry airmass is being reinforced from the north: the Canadian analysis shows a broad 1018-1023 hPa high over the Prairie provinces and western interior feeding suppressed dry air into the northern U.S. Plains, while a cold front trailing from a 1002 hPa low near British Columbia marks the leading edge of the eastern-Pacific trough digging in behind the departing warmth.

The centers of action all sit on the ridge's northern and western flanks. The most consequential today is the northern-stream convection: SPC carries a Slight risk from the northern and central Plains into the lower Ohio Valley, anchored by a morning MCS out of Iowa riding a 35-kt low-level jet into an extremely unstable airmass (MLCAPE near 4300 J/kg), with scattered severe wind and hail as the main threats and additional afternoon storms on the northern and central Plains. Running underneath that is the multi-day heavy-rain and flash-flood axis WPC flags from the High Plains through the Ohio Valley and central Appalachians along the stationary front. Out west, monsoon convection brings an excessive-rainfall threat to southern Arizona and New Mexico. In the tropics the East Pacific is busy — a system east-southeast of Hawaii at 90 percent worth Hawaiian attention and a second between Hawaii and Mexico at 70 percent — while the Atlantic ramps up with a Cabo Verde tropical wave at 80 percent and a subtropical low already producing gale-force winds east-northeast of Bermuda.

The upper-level structure ties this together and points to the change coming. The Air Mass RGB shows a sharp west-to-east color boundary from the central Rockies toward the Great Lakes marking the implied jet corridor, with the broad red-orange plume to its south being warm, dry ridge-top air rather than a stratospheric intrusion, and the deep convection over southern Iowa/northern Missouri firing along that baroclinic zone. The 500 mb analysis also plots a shallow trough between the Great Lakes ridge and a transient ridge cell over the Pacific Northwest, with a possible cutoff low near the Texas-Oklahoma border at a reported 532 dam — a value low enough, and flagged with enough caution by the analyst, that it should be read as a weak southern-Plains trough rather than a confidently closed feature. The near-term evolution is high-confidence: WPC's extended discussion keeps the southern-tier ridge in place through the weekend with the northern stream staying active, cyclogenesis over the northern Plains, and the heavy-rain focus shifting east into the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley, Mid-Atlantic and Northeast by Sunday into Monday. The genuine regime question is what happens beyond that. On the CONUS the two ensemble leads agree and tell a coherent story: both the 6-10 day (Aug 17-21) and 8-14 day (Aug 19-25) erase the western ridge, flatten the mid-latitude flow toward a more progressive regime, and retreat the ridge core southward toward the Southwest and northern Mexico — a real geographic contraction and loss of amplitude, not merely one shortwave passing through. Where the charts still cannot agree is at high latitudes: the 6-10 day shows a moderate positive height anomaly (about +9 dam) over the central Canadian Arctic near Hudson Bay, while the 8-14 day flips that same region to a deep trough (roughly -6 dam) with troughing pressing into the northern border states. That sign reversal across overlapping windows is a statement of low confidence, not a clean transition. The teleconnection cross-check is itself split — the AO has swung sharply positive (+0.37), nudging away from high-latitude blocking and toward the trough reading, while the NAO has reversed sharply negative (-0.90); with summer teleconnections only directionally suggestive, the height field has to carry the story, and here it genuinely does not settle the Arctic outcome.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America running close to the seasonal script: the North American Monsoon is active across the Southwest, Great Basin and southern Rockies, and severe-weather season is expressed as ridge-periphery, northern-stream convection along a wavy frontal zone rather than classic Plains supercell setups. The ENSO backdrop is a developing warm state — the ONI has climbed steadily out of last year's weak La Niña through neutral late winter into warm territory, reaching +1.39 C by May-July 2026, an El Niño-like configuration. That state typically favors the East Pacific while shear-suppressing the Atlantic, and today's tropics fit the split: a very active East Pacific (systems at 90 and 70 percent) against an Atlantic that, while quieter, is far from dormant, with the Cabo Verde wave at 80 percent and a subtropical low already producing gales as the basin builds toward its early-September climatological peak — a state that warrants monitoring rather than complacency.
synthesis.regional_notes: Two SPC mesoscale discussions are active under Watch 573 across Iowa and eastern Nebraska. MCD 1948 (through 1430Z) tracks a mesoscale convective vortex near the central Iowa I-80 corridor where a weakening cluster may re-intensify, capable of 55-70 mph gusts and hail to 1.75 inches; MCD 1947 notes the initial Omaha-area cluster weakening from mid-level inhibition even as strong gusts persist, with new development expected across central/southern Iowa (CAPE 2000+ J/kg). Away from the severe threat, watch the localized monsoon flash-flood risk over southern Arizona and New Mexico in burn scars and canyon terrain, and isolated severe gusts in the Lower Colorado River Valley. On the cool side, northern Montana along the Canadian border may see its coldest temperatures since June as the Prairie high and incoming Pacific trough combine.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 1200Z 12 August 2020 WPC surface analysis shows a complex multi-center pattern across the contiguous US. The most notable low pressure is a cluster of systems across the northern Rockies and High Plains, with centers reading near 1006-1009 mb over Montana and Wyoming, and an additional weak low near 1008 mb over the southern Rockies into New Mexico — these gradients are slack enough that frontal forcing rather than the pressure centers themselves is doing most of the dynamic work. A stationary or slow-moving front extends from the upper Midwest southwestward, with what appears to be a warm front arcing through the Great Lakes and a cold front trailing southward into Texas, where the tighter spacing of isobars along the frontal zone suggests the best-focused surface convergence on the chart. A strong high, reading near 1019-1020 mb, is centered over the southeastern Gulf Coast region, and its clockwise flow is feeding Gulf moisture northward into the Mississippi Valley and the active frontal zone, which is where the chart most clearly concentrates both moisture transport and surface lift. The Pacific coast shows a modest 1013-1016 mb high off Baja and slack gradients over California, consistent with suppressed onshore flow, while a separate 1018 mb high over Atlantic Canada is tightening the gradient along the northeastern seaboard and driving the offshore flow there.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Wednesday 12 August 2026 shows a broad high pressure ridge dominating much of central Canada, with centers labeled near 1023 hPa over what appears to be the western Canadian interior and 1018-1020 hPa in the central plains region, consistent with a suppressed, dry airmass across the Prairie provinces and into the northern Great Plains of the United States. A frontal zone — marked with a cold front symbol — extends from a low near 1002 hPa in the vicinity of the Pacific coast or BC interior southward and eastward into the northwestern United States, where it connects to a series of wave features; the isobar packing along this boundary suggests a locally tightened gradient and the implied ascent zone for convective or stratiform precipitation across that corridor. In the eastern part of the domain, a low center reading near 993 hPa sits well north, in what the projection places over the high Arctic or sub-Arctic region well above Hudson Bay, and should not be read as a provincial feature. Across the Great Lakes and into the northeastern US, isobars are relatively slack and frontal boundaries are diffuse, suggesting limited organized lift over Ontario and Quebec at this analysis time. The lower portion of the chart shows a complex of weak lows and quasi-stationary front segments over the central and southern United States that do not extend clearly into Canadian territory at this hour.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb valid 1200 UTC 12 August 2026, the dominant feature is a broad, amplified ridge centered over the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes region, with the core height values reaching approximately 588 dam and a concentrated bull's-eye of the warmest temperatures (around -14 to -15 C) collocated with heights near 568 dam over the Ohio Valley area — the brown shading indicates the ridge apex near 588 dam extending from roughly the central Plains northeastward into the Great Lakes. A second ridge cell is evident over the Pacific Northwest and interior British Columbia, with heights around 587-590 dam, creating a dual-ridge configuration across the western and central domains. Between these two ridges, a broad but relatively shallow trough axis runs from the northern Rockies southward through the central Plains, where a closed low center appears plotted near the Texas-Oklahoma border vicinity at approximately 532 dam — the closed contours around that H marker (which appears to be a 500 mb low symbol) suggest this is a genuine cutoff low, retaining closed circulation rather than an open wave, though the contour spacing is tight enough to warrant caution in reading the exact closing contour. A large surface high labeled H sits over the western Gulf of Mexico, separate from the upper-level pattern. The overall longwave configuration shows a high-amplitude, progressive-resistant pattern with the cutoff low anchored well south of the westerly flow and the ridge to its north implying a quasi-stationary dipole rather than a classic Rex block, since the anticyclonic center is not clearly stacked poleward of the low at the same longitude but instead displaced well to the northwest.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 12 August 2026 at 13:51Z shows a broad expanse of reddish-orange tones across the central and southern United States from the southern Plains eastward through the Deep South and into the Gulf of Mexico, consistent with a deep, dry upper-tropospheric airmass under what is likely a broad summertime ridge — this is dry subsident air, not a stratospheric intrusion. The most compelling dry intrusion signature appears as an elongated, more saturated orange-reddish streamer curling cyclonically around a trough evident over the central Plains and upper Midwest, where the sharp color boundary between the dry orange air to the south and the greener moister tones to the north marks the implied jet corridor running roughly from the central Rockies toward the Great Lakes. A cluster of deep convection with cold bright-white tops is visible over the upper Midwest near the southern Iowa and northern Missouri region, positioned along the southern edge of that boundary, consistent with convective development along the baroclinic zone. Across Cuba, Hispaniola, and the western Caribbean, scattered convective clusters with cold tops are embedded in broadly green tropical moist air. Along the U.S. East Coast from roughly the Carolinas northeastward, a narrow band of mid-to-upper cloud associated with the exiting synoptic system stretches offshore, while the green signature over the Southeast and Florida Peninsula confirms deep tropical moisture extending well inland.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB valid 12 Aug 2026 at 1340Z shows a broad expanse of green across the tropical belt from the eastern Pacific through Central America, the Caribbean, and into the Amazon basin, consistent with deep, moist tropical airmass. Scattered clusters of cold white cloud tops are visible over Colombia and the Panama-Costa Rica border region, with additional active convection over the Gulf of Mexico and the Yucatan Peninsula, suggesting organized deep convection possibly associated with an ITCZ disturbance or tropical wave passage. Across the Southern Ocean south of roughly 50S, a well-organized cyclonic swirl is visible southwest of southern Chile, marked by a tight comma-shaped cloud shield with a warm orange-red dry slot wrapping around its western flank — a compact, elongated dry intrusion on the cyclonic side of the flow consistent with a stratospheric or high-PV signature associated with that extratropical system. Across Canada and the high Arctic, the airmass transitions from blue-purple in the far north to greener tones over the Great Lakes region, with the sharpest color gradient — implying the polar airmass boundary and the implied jet corridor — running roughly from the Canadian Prairies toward Hudson Bay. The broad orange-red coloring over the subtropical eastern Pacific and subtropical South America likely reflects dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air beneath the Southern Hemisphere winter ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant signal on this outlook is a broad above-normal temperature probability covering virtually the entire southern tier from the Desert Southwest eastward through Texas, the Gulf Coast states, the Southeast, and into the mid-Atlantic, with the highest probabilities — 90-100 percent — centered over a core spanning roughly Arkansas, Mississippi, Tennessee, and adjacent portions of Louisiana and Alabama, indicating a very strong and confident warm signal there. A secondary 80-90 percent above-normal bull's-eye sits over southern Texas and extends into New Mexico and Oklahoma, and the above-normal signal weakens but remains at 40-60 percent across much of the interior West and the northern Plains, suggesting the above-normal regime is broad even if less certain away from the southern core. The lone below-normal signal of note in the contiguous states is a 50-60 percent probability oval centered over the Great Basin, covering roughly Nevada and Utah, with near-normal probabilities bridging it to the Pacific Northwest above-normal area — implying a trough-ridge-trough configuration at upper levels, with the Great Basin sitting under implied troughing while ridging dominates the South and East. Maine and far northern New England show a 50-60 percent below-normal signal, consistent with a downstream trough position at the northeastern periphery of what appears to be a persistent mid-tropospheric ridge dominating the South. The strength and spatial coherence of the 90-100 percent core, maintained six to ten days out, implies the CPC favors continuation of the current upper ridge anchored over the south-central states rather than a significant pattern break over this period.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
The chart is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly forecast, valid 17-21 August 2026, with heights in dam at 60 dam intervals and anomalies overlaid as dashed contours.

The dominant feature is a strongly positive height anomaly center located over the central Canadian Arctic, near the northern end of Hudson Bay and into the Queen Elizabeth Islands, where the anomaly contours reach +90 dam — however, that value is almost certainly a misread or a units issue, as a +90 dam anomaly would be physically absurd; the plotted dashed contours labeled 90, -30, -90 and similar values are more consistent with anomalies in meters (roughly +9, -3, -9 dam respectively when converted), which is the typical range for ensemble-mean 500 mb anomaly products. Reading the anomaly field in those terms, the Arctic high anomaly center near Hudson Bay is approximately +9 dam, a moderate positive signal. A negative anomaly region of roughly -3 dam sits over the Pacific Northwest and western Canada, with the -90 m (-9 dam equivalent) contour reaching into the Gulf of Alaska, indicating a trough axis implied across the northeastern Pacific and into British Columbia. Over the contiguous western United States, the anomaly field near zero to weakly negative suggests the positive height anomaly that might otherwise support a western ridge is largely absent, with the zero-anomaly line cutting across roughly the U.S.-Canada border from the Pacific coast eastward, meaning any prior western ridge amplification has retreated poleward or northeastward rather than holding over the western CONUS. The 500 mb height pattern shows a ridge axis arching from the central U.S. northeastward toward the Arctic high center, while a broad trough is implied across the Pacific and into the Pacific Northwest, and the relatively zonal, close spacing of height contours across the mid-latitudes of the lower 48 is consistent with a trend toward more progressive, less amplified flow over the contiguous United States for this period.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast valid 19-25 August 2026, made 11 August 2026, with green solid contours for heights at 60 m intervals and dashed contours for anomalies (red positive, blue negative). The dominant feature is a deep negative height anomaly centered over the central Canadian Arctic, roughly over the Boreal Archipelago area northwest of Hudson Bay, where the anomaly contours reach -60 dam on the chart label — but that reading would be extraordinary and almost certainly represents -60 m (about -6 dam), consistent with a strong but not unprecedented trough; the closed 534 dam height contour there confirms a pronounced cyclonic circulation. There is no meaningful positive height anomaly indicated over western Canada, the northern Rockies, or the northern Plains; instead, the height contours across that entire corridor show a strong meridional gradient as they wrap around the Arctic low, with the implied flow pattern delivering a persistent troughing influence across much of interior Canada well into the northern U.S. border states. A broad, relatively weak ridge axis is implied across the southwestern U.S. and northern Mexico, where the 534 dam contour closes over the Gulf Coast states and the height field flattens across the southern tier, suggesting the ridge core has retreated southward well away from the northern Rockies rather than holding a position there. The positive anomaly dashed contours (red) are most prominent over the western North Atlantic and over the Greenland-Baffin region on the chart's eastern flank, consistent with a downstream ridge flanking the dominant Arctic trough.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Dangerous heat dome building from Southwest into Central Plains and Southeast through Friday, with heat indices 105-115 degrees and potential record highs. Stationary front along northern fringe driving daily severe thunderstorms and flash flooding threats from High Plains through Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. Western U.S. cooling trend underway with below-normal temperatures arriving today, expanding Thursday as heat dome exits. Afternoon storms possible across West with excessive rainfall risk in southern Arizona and New Mexico. Montana highs near Canadian border may reach coldest levels since June.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
Slight risk of severe thunderstorms from northern/central Plains to lower Ohio Valley. Primary hazards are severe gusts and large hail.

Morning thunderstorm clusters ongoing from Iowa into Ohio Valley with the strongest over eastern Iowa moving into Illinois. Very moist, extremely unstable airmass (4300 J/kg MLCAPE) near a 35-kt low-level jet supports gradual intensification with scattered severe wind damage expected. Considerable uncertainty on additional cluster development. Outflow into Kentucky will inhibit eastward spread.

Northern/Central Plains: Moderate buoyancy with 30+ kt effective shear will organize afternoon/evening scattered storms, threatening large hail and severe gusts. Low confidence on specific severe corridors.

Lower Michigan into NY/PA: 35+ kt effective shear with veering winds and 1000-1500 J/kg MLCAPE supports isolated to scattered storms posing damaging gust and marginal hail risk.

Tennessee Valley/Southeast: Midday storm development in very moist, unstable airmass with high precipitable water supports isolated strong downdrafts capable of wind damage.

Lower Colorado River Valley: Widely scattered storms possible with isolated severe gust potential.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary:
Two mesoscale discussions track severe weather under Watch 573 across Iowa and eastern Nebraska through mid-morning August 12.

MCD 1948 (valid through 1430Z) focuses on central Iowa near the I-80 corridor where a weakening thunderstorm cluster spreading from the Missouri River may re-intensify. A mesoscale convective vortex with associated pressure rises is maintaining CAPE and wind shear supportive of organized convection capable of producing severe hail and damaging downbursts (55-70 mph gusts, hail to 1.75 inches).

MCD 1947 (valid through 1030Z) describes the initial intense cluster undergoing notable weakening due to mid-level inhibition and weak low-level forcing, though strong gusts persist near/north of Omaha through early morning. New development expected across central/southern Iowa as a convectively augmented perturbation moves east-southeastward, with potential for vigorous upscale growth into another organized cluster capable of severe hail and strong to severe gusts. CAPE values 2000+ J/kg support the threat.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
**ATLANTIC:** Tropical wave 900 miles west-southwest of Cabo Verde has 80 percent chance of forming depression within 48 hours as it moves west-northwestward; conditions favorable for development. Subtropical low 1050 miles east-northeast of Bermuda is already producing tropical-storm-force winds and likely to briefly organize into tropical storm moving east-northeastward. African tropical wave near West Africa coast has only 20-30 percent development odds over next week.

**EAST PACIFIC:** Low pressure 1050 miles east-southeast of Hawaiian Islands expected to form depression or storm within 24 hours (90 percent chance) while moving west-northwestward; Hawaii should monitor closely. Separate system midway between Hawaii and Mexico coast has 70 percent chance of depression formation within 48 hours, though conditions deteriorate late week.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ONI values show the transition from weak La Niña conditions to approaching neutral and warming waters through early 2026. OND 2025 and NDJ 2025 maintain slight negative anomalies around -0.6°C, characteristic of residual La Niña. The trend reverses into positive anomaly territory by FMA 2026, strengthening substantially through spring and early summer 2026. By MJJ 2026, anomalies reach +1.39°C, suggesting transition toward warm or El Niño-like conditions. The warming trajectory is steady and consistent across all successive three-month periods.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA is weakly negative, falling over the past week to -0.70 (7-day mean), suggesting reduced western ridge/eastern trough support. AO has swung sharply positive (now +0.37, up from -0.05), indicating a shift away from high-latitude blocking. NAO has reversed sharply negative to -0.90, dropping from +0.19 the prior week, favoring potential eastern cutoff development. Summer teleconnections are directionally suggestive rather than canonical. The recent reversals in AO and NAO merit attention for pattern shifts.
